name: ats2-postiats
desc: Programming language with formal specification features
why: A dependently typed language with formal proofs built into the code, a strange and rarely seen corner of programming language design.

brief.what_it_is: ATS (ATS/Postiats, the ATS2 implementation) is a statically typed programming language that its author describes as unifying implementation with formal specification. It is call-by-value and ML-inspired at its core, with dependent and linear types built on the Applied Type System framework. The homepage shows small programs that print text, catch an out-of-bounds list subscript at compile time, use templates for code reuse, and solve the N-Queens puzzle with combinators. The scout's executables (myatscc, patscc, patsopt) are the compiler front ends, but the homepage does not describe them.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames ATS as a way to get the power of types and theorem-proving into practical programming. Its homepage says it aims to "enforce precision in practical programming" and to "facilitate refinement-based software development", and it also positions ATS as a teaching tool for type theory.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says ATS/LF, a subsystem, supports interactive theorem-proving in which proofs are built as total functions, so programming and proving are intertwined in the same source. Linear types track resources, which the homepage credits for low memory footprint and for safe explicit memory management and pointer arithmetic. The current ATS2 compiler is itself written in ATS1 (ATS/Anairiats), at over 180K lines.
brief.install_notes: The homepage has a Downloads section with pages for requirements, precompiled packages, installation through source compilation, ATS2-contrib, ATS2-include, and install scripts, but I did not follow them, so I cannot report specifics. The homepage also offers an in-browser "Try ATS on-line" option that needs no install.
brief.standout: Dependent and linear types sit inside a language that compiles to efficient native code, and proofs are written as ordinary total functions in the same source file as the program. Its own examples show compile-time bounds checking and a C++-style template system.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage has no release date, version number, or recent-news item that I could see, and I did not open the Downloads or changelog pages to check for a release or commit date. The site is a personal academic page, and its menu includes a "Home(old)" entry.
brief.caveats: The homepage calls ATS "feature-rich (like C++)" and says that learning it means "spend a substantial amount of time" on unfamiliar concepts. I did not verify the license, platform support, or build requirements, since I did not fetch the installation pages. The executables listed in the brew metadata are not described on the homepage. The brew caveats field is empty. The scout's note calls it "a strange and rarely seen corner of programming language design", which is the scout's framing, not the author's.
quotes: ATS is a statically typed programming language that unifies implementation with formal specification.
Unleashing the Potentials of Types and Templates!
ATS is feature-rich (like C++). Prior knowledge of functional programming based on ML and imperative programming based on C can be a big plus for learning ATS.
